periods.analysis: Harborview closed 93.4% of citywide service requests on time, comfortably above the >=90% target and a strong starting point for the FY25 reporting cycle. This quarter’s result reflects steady performance across HarborHelp 311 intake, Public Works right-of-way crews on Routes N-3 and S-2, and Parks’ summer restroom and litter tickets along the Seawall Loop. The data quality check was encouraging: duplicate sidewalk and graffiti cases were consolidated before month-end, which helped departments get fair credit for the work they completed. For Council, the headline is simple and positive: residents are getting timely responses while the city keeps pace with fast-growth demand.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the HarborHelp weekly aging report every Tuesday at 10 a.m., with department coordinators clearing all requests older than 12 business days before Friday close. Extend the Q3 workflow by adding a standard closure-note template for Public Works, Parks, and Code Compliance so resolution quality remains as strong as the 93.4% timeliness result. I recommend we use this quarter as the baseline for the dashboard trend line and publish department-level drilldowns in the next Council packet.

periods.analysis: The citywide resolution rate was 92.9%, down 0.5 percentage points from 93.4% in 2024-Q3, but still green and above the >=90% target. The small dip is understandable: December holiday staffing, coastal storm debris calls, and year-end permit counter questions pushed more tickets into the 8-to-12-day window. Departments still performed well, especially Solid Waste and Streets, which used the Bayshore Debris Sweep vendor route to close high-volume storm-related requests without creating a backlog. My read is watchful but confident: the system absorbed a seasonal surge and kept residents served on time.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by pre-loading holiday coverage calendars into HarborHelp before Thanksgiving next year, so dispatchers see alternate owners instead of parking requests in general queues. Extend the Bayshore Debris Sweep playbook to the North Marina and Hillcrest routes for any future storm-response weeks. For the Q1 reporting cycle, I recommend a quick audit of open Q4 carryover cases by case type, with special attention to tree-limb and streetlight tickets.

periods.analysis: Harborview improved to 93.7%, up 0.8 percentage points from 92.9% in 2024-Q4 and again above the >=90% target. The rebound shows that the Q4 carryover review worked: Facilities closed a cluster of Civic Center HVAC requests, and Transportation cleared signal-timing tickets tied to controllers HV-SIG-014 and HV-SIG-022. Intake quality also improved after the January refresher for front-desk and call-center staff, with fewer cases needing reassignment after the first 24 hours. This is the kind of clean, department-friendly progress I want in front of Council: modest process discipline, visible resident benefit.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the improvement by keeping the 24-hour triage standard for all new HarborHelp cases and sending the reassignment report to department liaisons every Wednesday. Extend the January refresher into a 20-minute onboarding module for seasonal Parks staff before spring hiring ramps up. I recommend flagging signal, sidewalk, and facility tickets as priority cohorts in Q2 so we can see whether the 93.7% rate is broad-based or concentrated in a few work groups.

periods.analysis: The resolution rate rose to 95%, up 1.3 percentage points from 93.7% in 2025-Q1 and the strongest performance in this sequence so far. That green result reflects real operational follow-through: the Spring Clean Harbor campaign bundled graffiti, illegal dumping, and park amenity requests by geography instead of sending crews back and forth across town. Community Development also helped by routing permit-related resident questions through the new Permit Assist queue, which kept non-inspection service requests from sitting in the wrong bucket. With growth pressure still real, this quarter gives us a credible story that better routing and cleaner data can raise service levels without pretending demand is easy.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 95% result by keeping geographic batching for graffiti, dumping, and parks requests through the summer visitor season, especially along Harbor Boulevard, Pier District, and East Bluffs. Extend the Permit Assist queue rules into Code Compliance nuisance cases where residents often submit mixed permit-and-enforcement questions. I recommend capturing the Spring Clean Harbor crew map and queue rules as a standard operating procedure before staff rotate into July vacation schedules.

periods.analysis: Harborview remained green at 92.6%, but the rate decreased 2.4 percentage points from 95% in 2025-Q2, so this is a friendly nudge moment. The dip aligns with summer tourism volume, back-to-school traffic complaints, and a higher number of coastal access maintenance requests after the August king tides. Even with that surge, the city stayed above the >=90% target because Public Works added two Saturday response blocks on Seaview Route W-1 and Parks reassigned the Beach Crew to close shower, bench, and trash-can requests in batches. The result is still strong, but the trend tells us not to coast on the excellent Q2 peak.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green performance by keeping the Saturday response blocks available during peak visitor weeks, but schedule them from the aging report rather than first-in, first-out alone. Extend the Beach Crew batching model to school-zone sign and crosswalk requests each August, with Transportation pre-tagging those cases as a seasonal cohort. I recommend a Q4 watch-item on requests aged 10-plus business days so we correct the downward movement before it becomes a pattern.

periods.analysis: The citywide service request resolution rate was 91.5%, down 1.1 percentage points from 92.6% in 2025-Q3, while still green against the >=90% target. This is the second consecutive quarterly decline, so I would frame it for Council as meeting standard but needing disciplined follow-through. The main pressure points were year-end staffing gaps, leaf and drain inlet requests in the older Harbor Heights grid, and a temporary vendor delay on streetlight repairs tied to Lumina contract WO-4471. The good news is that departments did not lose the handle: HarborHelp escalation notes show supervisors were actively moving aging cases before they breached the service window.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green status by requiring each department to review its 10-plus-business-day list twice weekly through January, not just at month-end. Extend the Harbor Heights leaf-and-drain route plan to include asset-tagged inlets HH-DI-118 through HH-DI-146 before the next heavy rain period. I recommend Procurement and Public Works confirm Lumina’s streetlight parts inventory by January 15 so vendor delay does not drag Q1 performance below the recent trend.

periods.analysis: Harborview improved to 93.5%, up 2.0 percentage points from 91.5% in 2025-Q4 and solidly green above the >=90% target. This rebound is exactly what we wanted after two softer quarters: departments used the January aging-list cadence, and HarborHelp closed old duplicates before they distorted the open-case count. Public Works also resolved the Lumina streetlight backlog on corridors HV-LT-31 through HV-LT-44, while Customer Service reduced misrouted sanitation requests after updating the intake script. The chronological story is reassuring: when the dashboard pointed to slippage, staff adjusted quickly and residents saw faster resolution.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the rebound by making the twice-weekly aging review a standing practice for all departments through the end of FY26, with exceptions reported before the quarterly close. Extend the duplicate-case cleanup protocol to mobile-app submissions, where residents often file repeat pothole or streetlight requests with slightly different locations. I recommend documenting the Q1 recovery actions in the Council narrative appendix so the 93.5% result is tied to visible management action, not luck.

periods.analysis: The resolution rate increased again to 94%, up 0.5 percentage points from 93.5% in 2026-Q1 and continuing the green recovery above the >=90% target. The improvement was broad enough to trust: Parks, Transportation, and Code Compliance all benefited from cleaner routing, while the new Resident Response Cohort for Spanish-language callers reduced follow-up delays in the South Harbor service area. Seasonal spring demand was handled without repeating last year’s Q3 softness, helped by preassigned crews for potholes on Route E-4 and park amenity checks before Memorial Day. For a fast-growing AA-rated city, this is the right service-excellence posture: responsive, measurable, and still humble about keeping the operating rhythm tight.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 94% performance by locking in pre-season crew assignments for visitor, pothole, and park-amenity requests at least four weeks before each peak period. Extend the Resident Response Cohort language-access workflow to Vietnamese and Tagalog call-back templates by the next quarterly reporting deadline. I recommend setting a management stretch watch of 94% or better for the next two quarters while keeping the formal target at >=90%, so departments are encouraged without being set up for noise-driven misses.

periods.analysis: Service request resolution improved to 91.8%, above the 90% target, while other citywide outcomes remain mixed.
periods.recommendations: Continue queue checks and publish aging categories so timely closure remains credible.
